utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could we have the witness, please. Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. As the witness is being brought in, with your leave I have something to say about our witness list. First, I'd like to say that we have supplied a new list for the next week, and the protective measures requested for those witnesses. We have also supplied our colleagues in the Prosecution with the same list and we are envisaging but I am looking forward to your instructions. We expect that after this witness is over, we have two more witnesses and we believe that their direct examination will last a very short time, perhaps even less than the witness yesterday. If we can manage to finish them today and we'd really like to ask that everybody makes an effort so that we do finish them, these five people have been here for the past week, they have their tickets for Sunday and are hoping to leave on Sunday, so if it would be possible I'd like to have them finished. Next week I believe we shall have only four working days because I believe we will not be working Friday. We have a list of five witnesses and they will be arriving Sunday. My question to you, Your Honours, is do you think that this estimate of five witnesses for the next week suffices or do you think that we should perhaps try to bring some more witnesses over? Because we have to inform the Victims and Witnesses Unit that these are the witnesses for next week or perhaps do you think we should try to get some other people in here? And then again we have to inform the victims and witnesses unit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much for your information, Mr. Par. And I've already said that I'm not that optimistic as your team, thinking that we could finish five witnesses this week. In my view, we will try our best but I could not guarantee that we could finish the last witness today. So in this case, there might be some delay, so the last witness for this week might sit a little bit longer next Monday. So in this case, with the five witnesses next week, I think we have enough witnesses for the next week. But we will try our best to see how far we could go with this afternoon's proceedings. Yes, could we have the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Bos: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you could say that, yes, I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Bos, you may start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I have a few more questions for you this afternoon, and I'd like to start off by asking were you active in combat during the war against the Serbs starting in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time I was still full-time employed, and I was responsible for a group of people and our duty was to rescue the property that belonged to our company, what was left to simply salvage whatever was left, so that we were a work team and we were getting things out, all the inventory, all the stocks that we had, and we then used it during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was your son, was he active in that war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I understood you right, you testified that during that time, your father died? Is it correct that he got killed during this -- in this war against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately after the beginning of the aggression, the Serb aggression, my father wasn't living with me. He was in his family house in the place that I was born in, and some formations, some armed military formations came up and without any announcement whatsoever, took him out and fired five bullets into him, a whole round of five bullets and he was an old man of 85.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these were Serbian military formations who killed your father?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb military formations, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to another topic. Witness, is it a fair statement to say that your family had a very good relationship with the Martinovic family, since you lived in the same neighbourhood and your son was about the same age as Vinko and you knew each other for about 40 years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also correct that you had a very close friendship with Mr. Vinko Martinovic's father, Ivan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We met, we socialised, before the war and during the war. I mean quite normal human relations as it should be between neighbours, caring for each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you to this date still good friends with Ivan Martinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I'd say we are even better friends than we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, witness, was it Ivan who asked you whether you could come here to testify in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the indictment was published, Ivan did come and asked me if I would mind, if necessary, of my own will, since I survived the war and since I lived in their neighbourhood, would I mind if I went to testify in this case about what I knew about him during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Bos, just turn off the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Witness, do you know whether Mr. Ivan Martinovic also approached other persons to come here and testify?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've stated that your son was about the same age as Vinko. What -- was your son good friends with Vinko? What was their relationship?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, they moved in a narrow circle and like all young people, they were pals, they went out together. And then when they were small boys, they went together, and then as they grew up, so in that sense, they were on good terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they in the same school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, they were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would your son often visit the Martinovic family or would Vinko come and visit your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know what? They were young people and they would just get together, perhaps they'd bump into each other in the street and then go somewhere together. It's not that they came to -- that they exchanged home visits, that they came to the house, but they went out with their girlfriends and all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your son doing in 1993 when the war started against the -- between the Croats and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was -- he lived with me. He had barely married and had a little daughter, and he was there in the family circle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he join any army in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he stay in West Mostar the whole of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: In September, 1993, he was issued a guarantee by his wife's relatives in Germany, and went to Germany via Zagreb and he stayed there until 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the period before he left Mostar, did he often see Vinko during that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not as often as before, but we -- I would see him now and then, when Vinko offered us some security and assistance. I saw him more often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw Vinko more often than your son did? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, yes, because listen, it was dangerous to go out into the street, so I didn't have much opportunity until I joined the civil defence because you don't know when you're in the street, but when I joined the civil defence and when I started moving around more than I used to but he, since he did not join it, it was mostly at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let's move to the 9th of May, 1993. You stated that you heard shelling in the morning and that -- I think you said that you first felt that the Serbs attacked Mostar again; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, when I heard those strange shouts and some funny din in the yard, I thought that the Muslims and Croats were engaging in general mobilisation in order to offer resistance to the Serbs because until then, everything was fine, I mean between the Muslims and the Croats. All the actions, I mean, were done together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you find out that it wasn't in fact a mobilisation but that it was a war between the Croats and the Muslims? Was that on the same day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, that same day, I could see that the same day because the media began saying something about that, so that I realised that that was it, that a split had occurred between Muslims and that a conflict had broken out that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it also on that same day that you approached Ivan Martinovic for protection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that same day, because it was too risky to go out. There were people milling about, a strange situation, civilians, troops, so that no, I didn't do it that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how long after the 9th of May did you actually -- went to see the father of Vinko Martinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first through some Croat friends, who could move about, I let him know that I was there, and could he do whatever he could, in case something bad happened, if he could protect me, me and my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was this a few days after the 9th of May or several weeks after the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, I didn't see him for a few days, but then when I was around those buildings, I came across him and we talked for a while, and I then spoke to him in those words which I have just presented to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct to say that you got the protection you've asked for because Ivan Martinovic talked to his son about your concerns?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you got the protection, you wanted protection from the Martinovic family, is it correct that you got the protection because Ivan Martinovic spoke with Vinko and asked him to protect you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm quite sure of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you again explain to the Court why you actually went to the Martinovics to ask for protection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know what, when you are friends with somebody and when you, you know, become close, somewhat freer, because you couldn't really turn to just anybody at that time, even though I had other Croat friends, but somehow I felt that at that particular moment, because Mr. Vinko during the Serb conflict and so on, that he was on good terms and said, "Do you need anything, need any help or something?" I mean I wasn't working so that I thought it would be safest if I went to him. But I had some other Croat friends and perhaps I could have gone to them but I did -- well, I knew him and somehow I felt that I -- that it would be all right and I was free to talk to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could it be that you heard that Vinko Martinovic had a -- had some sort of military position in the area which could make him control other soldiers in the neighbourhood, that you approached the Martinovics for protection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was in a unit, and Tuta, he was also in a unit, which was in that area, and then naturally, being a soldier, and how shall I put it, physically rather fit man who was capable of protecting one, and that is what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: My colleague Ms. Pinter who speaks fluent Croatian has just informed me that in line 21 in the witness's answer, it came across on the screen, the answer, well, meaning Mr. Martinovic was in a unit, and Tuta he was also in a unit. Ms. Pinter says that he did not say that in Croatian and it must be a problem in translation. He never mentioned Tuta in his language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bos, maybe you could ask your question again to make sure the answer is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, maybe I should ask.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you refer to the name Tuta in your answer, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've said that Mr. Martinovic was a member of a unit. Do you know the name of that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday when my learned friend asked you why you felt safe under the protection of Mr. Vinko Martinovic, you stated three reasons. You said that he was a uniformed soldier, that he had determination, and as a third reason you said his readiness to physically oppose somebody at any given moment. Why did you give that last reason? I'd like to know why did you give that last reason? How did you know that Vinko was capable of using physical violence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, I meant all those groups which at that time, like that, did rounds and did certain things, which were not allowed under any rules, and I think that Vinko was physically fit to be able to resist such Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. people in such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I was waiting for the witness to finish, so that I wouldn't lead the witness but in Mr. Bos's question, there was a -- or at least that is how it was interpreted to us, that Vinko Martinovic was ready to physically oppose. I think that this was a wrong word, because what we heard was physical violence. But I think that the word was misused, that the witness did not mean physical violence. He meant fitness. The witness never used the word "violence."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that the witness never used the word "violence." Let's change it into physical "fitness."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you spoke about an occasion that soldiers broke into your home. Could you give us the date when this was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you mean the 9th of May or later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the second occasion that soldiers broke into your home.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It happened sometime in August. Yes. It could have been 9.00 or half past 9.00 in the evening. Somebody rang my door bell and I opened the door and there were two men there, one was uniformed and another one was in civilian clothes. They wanted my particulars, my IDs, and the rest, and of my whole family's and I gave it to them. It was all happening in the anteroom, on the staircase, on the landing, and then we had this conversation, what and how, they told me to go with them, and when I asked, where is your son," my wife said, "With Vinko" and when they said, "Which Vinko?" And she said, "Vinko Martinovic Stela, why?" And it was then that they paused and then I could see in their faces that they realised they were doing something that they shouldn't and then they said, "Fine," gave me back the papers and sort of showing, well, perhaps we've made a mistake but we'll drop by later on again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were two men one man in uniform and one man in civilian clothes, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the man in the uniform, did you recognise the uniform, what kind of uniform did he wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time, I didn't really pay much attention but it looked just regular one, a camouflage uniform like the one that those armed units wore at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it have some sort of patch on the sleeve?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I understand you right when you say that these -- this soldier and this civilian did not dare to do anything to you and your family when your wife mentioned Vinko's name and explained that he was a friend of your son's?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I felt that they suddenly felt insecure for being there, something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, yesterday you testified -- and you don't know the name of the unit but you said that you knew other members of this unit, of which Stela was a member. Could you give us the names of the other men you know from this unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can perhaps name one or two men that I knew who were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mladen Colak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please spell his last name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: M-L-A-D-A-N, C-O-L-A-K.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you knew another name as well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember now. These are the boys from the neighbourhood, but not our immediate neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this Mladen Colak was somebody who also lived in your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you briefly spoke yesterday about the civil defence unit which you joined, and I didn't really understand. When was this unit formed? Was this during the war in 1993 or before or after?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civil defence units were established immediately after the Serb aggression and since I had my work duty in my company, I was not involved in the units until that time, until the time when the conflict between Croats and Muslims broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when did you get involved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 9th of May, when my work duty in the company ceased. This is when I joined the units of the civil defence, in the local commune, in the area where I lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm trying to understand here because, so you're saying on the 9th of May, when the war broke out between the Croats and Muslims, you joined this civil defence unit and you testified yesterday that this civil defence unit contained both Muslims, Croats and Serbs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's correct. There were Serbs there. The Serbs who remained there, who lived as our neighbours. Even in the course of the conflict with the Serbs, there were some there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so do I understand correct that this civil defence unit was sort of a neighbourhood unit of civilians living in the neighbourhood and trying to protect the neighbourhood -- the neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were civilian formations. It was not a reserve military formation of any kind. It was their task to offer protection and to provide food and all the rest that came in, to ensure just distribution and also to assist if there was a power outage or if the water supply was cut, to repair things that needed to be repaired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's correct that you -- both you and Vinko's father, Ivan Martinovic, were active in this unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were quite a few of us there. These were all the people who were not involved elsewhere. We all had the obligation to report and to assist in those really different times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, there was something in your statement yesterday that struck me when you spoke about the civil defence, because at one time you said that you had an opportunity to meet Mr. Vinko Martinovic himself and then you stated, I'll quote from the transcript, "He was always very forthcoming and he talked with me and it meant a great deal to me at the time. Because even a nice greeting was also a major prize. And he was always ready for that." My question is, Witness, is why is it -- is even a nice greeting from somebody what you have seen grown up in your neighbourhood a major prize for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, when you have a state of war, and if somebody is in a position to assist you while people at the same time are changing, I felt that Vinko had remained the same, and when you are in danger in any way, when you're under threat, it wasn't just Vinko. I felt really good if any Croat said hello to me. It simply made me feel better and let alone if somebody provided you assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you afraid of Mr. Vinko Martinovic at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I was not afraid. I felt that he was trying to help me, and that he would help me in as much as he would be able to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, so you lived in West Mostar during the whole period of 1993. You said that you were a member of the civil defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever witness any instances where Muslims were evicted from their houses by soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see that with my own eyes but I did hear that people would come and evict people, but I was never present at any such occasion or any such incident. I tried to avoid being put in any danger, in any situation that might be potentially dangerous to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you testified that yesterday is it correct that there was talk among the population that Stela's unit was involved in this practice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did hear about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know what happened to the apartments where these Muslims were evicted from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The apartments that the Muslims left were filled with people I didn't know, least ways I who lived there would meet those people but I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what ethnicities -- what ethnicity did these people have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they were predominantly, as far as I know, Croats, refugees from other areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, and this is going to be my last question: Did you ever during that period that were you in West Mostar in 1993 see soldiers loot apartments?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you want to see such a thing, you have to be present there. I didn't eyewitness anyone taking things away, because at that time, I was not concentrating on that. That was not something that I focused on. I was focusing on my personal security.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No re-examination. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Witness, for coming to give your evidence. The usher will show you out of the room. We all wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, I think that street map with the original number P11.18 was marked by the witness. Mr. Par, are you going to tender it into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. We would like to tender it into evidence. That would be Defence Exhibit D2/28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I guess there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I let the witness make some marks on this exhibit as well, but we are happy to keep it as a Defence Exhibit as long as in the minutes it will be noted that the Prosecution asked for some marks as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. It is admitted into evidence as D2/28. That should be under seal, I guess. Yes, could we have the next witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric? Your direct examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Seric:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I will be referring to you as Witness, although you will be assigned a pseudonym because you did request this protective measure and this has been granted to you. I have something to ask you. Since we also have the voice distortion as the protective measure, I would like to ask you not to start answering my question before I have switched off my microphone. To verify that, you can look at my microphone and see whether the red light is on. If the red light is not on, you can give your answer. Before that, Ms. Usher will give you a piece of paper with your full name on it. Please do not read it out loud. Just confirm whether this is indeed your name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please give us some basic details about yourself, without revealing your name and without revealing in any way your identity?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, if I may request that we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please tell all of us here, and in particular the Trial Chamber, what happened to you personally during the conflict or rather when the JNA and the Serb army attacked Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: When the Serb aggression started, right during the first few days, I went to the 4th Battalion as a volunteer, and I remained there throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you during the conflict between the BH Army and the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: I remained in the 4th Battalion, so the same thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Vinko Martinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How well do you know him? And since when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: I've known him since my childhood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him at the time when the JNA and the Serb army attacked Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what his role was in that war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: At that time, he was the commander of a unit. I think it was called HOS, H-O-S, and he played a prominent role in that war, because of his great courage and his fighting spirit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to how he treated Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know in which way he treated Muslims in relation to this HOS unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: He treated them completely normally, the same way as before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what was the ethnic composition of this HOS unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Well, to a considerable extent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: I think that 40 to 50 per cent of the personnel in his unit were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the way Vinko Martinovic treat you personally change throughout this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: No, never, not even for a second.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the day when the conflict broke out between the BH Army and the Croatian Defence Council in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: I think it was on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us very briefly what happened during that day, the things that you yourself observed or heard, and that you personally experienced?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: The night before, I was on duty in the battalion, so that I spent that evening at home, sleeping. In the morning, I was awakened by fierce shooting. I got up, didn't know what was happening. I got into my car and went straight to my battalion. And there, they told me that the conflict broke out between the BH Army and the HVO. I spent the entire day in the battalion. It was a pretty chaotic situation. There was shooting everywhere. In the evening, I went back home and I think that I met Vinko somewhere in Balinovac. I asked him, "Well, friend, what is going on?" He said, "I don't know anything. You can see yourself, nobody can tell where the shooting is coming from. The town is on fire. If you are afraid, you can go to Jagoda. My mother was in Jagoda." I went back to the battalion and stayed there until quite late. So that would be more or less that day, the way I remember it, the day when the conflict between the BH Army and the HVO started.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there is an interpretation error. When the witness told us about his conversation between himself and Vinko Martinovic, when he told him about his mother, Jagoda. In fact Jagoda is not his mother but Vinko Martinovic's mother. That's the name of Vinko Martinovic's mother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric, you may ask a question about that, bearing in mind the protective measures for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you, who Jagoda is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Jagoda is Vinko's mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you, as a Muslim Bosniak, see this conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: First of all, as a human being, I took this conflict very hard. I couldn't believe what was happening. Although there were some indications that this might happen, because the BH Army was already -- had already been regrouping its positions and withdrawing from the staffs in the town, although not many people believed that this would happen. But in the end, the thing that happened happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please repeat, what was your unit, your military formation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: I was in the unit that was called the 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you feel personally? Did you feel safe? And do you have any knowledge as to how your neighbours, Muslim neighbours, felt, the ones that you knew? I'm referring to the area that was under the control of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: I myself felt safe, and all my neighbours, Muslim neighbours, who lived there, had they not felt safe, they would have left, I presume. Mostly all of them remained there, apart from just a few people who left right at the beginning of the conflict. And these people are still there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally, or your family, experience any kind of unpleasantness or pressure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge of the fact that Vinko Martinovic had expelled anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what his role was at the time? Where was he, what he was doing, in what unit was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Vinko Martinovic was the commander of a unit that was called Mrmak. And they held positions right on the Bulevar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now like to show you an aerial photograph, if you can recognise whether the position that his unit held is on the picture? And that would be Prosecution Exhibit 14.5. And it would be our Exhibit D2/29. Witness, could you take the pointer and show us which part of the front line, or rather the separation line, was manned by Vinko Martinovic's unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: This part here. This is the health centre. This is Bulevar. And Vinko, Vinko was here. So this is the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, I could barely hear the witness. I do not know if you received any interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you now take the marker and make circle -- make a circle around that area that you showed us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: [marks] I've done it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point at the segment of the separation line manned by your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: You cannot see it here because there are these streets, but it's down here to -- moving left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. We won't need this photograph any more. You said that you kept a workshop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did it serve for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Well, it was a locksmith, a metal working shop. We repaired cars, locks, doors, minor repairs, maintenance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the detainees from the Heliodrom were brought to the base of Vinko Martinovic's unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that? Do you have any specific example?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Specifically, my half brother was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. President, could we go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, are you familiar with the charges against Mr. Martinovic? And if so, how?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I'm not sure I could quote it but I saw it in the press, I watch television so I more or less know what it is about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you seek protective measures, voice and facial protection?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go into private session once again, please, Mr. President? Don't answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was my last question, Mr. President, thank you very much?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have five minutes left. I suggest that we make a break here. Is that agreeable to both parties? Yes. We'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, cross-examination, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Scott:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you a few questions. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the witness could please be shown a copy of Exhibit 11.18, please? It shouldn't be broadcast outside the courtroom but as Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. long as nobody can see it, it doesn't --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I know you've told us that you came from [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps again we will go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will go back to the open session. We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in a summary of your anticipated testimony that was provided to us, there are references that there were various criminal groups moving around your neighbourhood, and I'd like to ask you about that. Were there groups during 1993, as the fighting between the Croats and Muslims was going on, were there criminal groups that were operating in your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Well, at that time, it was in existence, but I think to a lesser degree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it says that you approached -- you had approached Stela one or more times to seek protection from these various criminal groups. So did you in fact seek protection from these criminal groups or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: I don't think that I said that I sought protection against criminal groups, but merely that I asked him, "Well, my friend, what is going on?" Something to that effect, but nobody could defend themselves against those groups because there were so many people who were foreigners, who nobody knew. Let me give you a specific example. A Deutz truck was taken away from my neighbour. Now, who I ask you would come out and stand in front of a handful of armed people and tell them anything? And then Vinko came right at that moment, asked me what was going on, I said, well, they are trying to take away this man's car. And then he said, "Well, what are you doing, guys?" And they said, "Well, we need this car." And then he said, "Please, let the car be." And they did. God knows how many groups, such groups, there were. It's impossible to tell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, these individuals who were about to take the car that you said Mr. Martinovic stopped, were these soldiers? Were they in uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: They had uniforms but it is true that everybody was able to obtain uniforms. It doesn't mean that they were members of a unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you think at the time that they were soldiers or did you think they were just individuals acting as criminals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: At that time, I thought that they were probably soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, also in a summary that we were provided with, it indicated that one of the ways that you were protected, that Muslim families were protected, was by giving them documents. For example, documents establishing them as being members of Stela's unit. Did you ever know about that happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any instances where Mr. Martinovic, Stela, provided you or your family or to your knowledge other Muslims with some sort of documentation or documents for the purpose of protecting them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: I was a bit afraid because of my shop, because I did jobs for my unit, for his units and for many other units, whoever would come there. I took a paper from him and I put it on my shop, indicating that the shop was doing the jobs for the 4th Battalion, for his unit, and for another unit, I think. Simply in order for the criminals to be afraid, because they felt differently if they saw a list of such units. They would then be afraid to steal anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, following on that, what sort of list or documentation, then, were you given to have for the purpose of having that effect, that is of as you say, scaring, making these people to be afraid to bother you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Well, it was just a white paper, certifying that I was -- that my shop was doing jobs for the battalion and that I myself was a member of that battalion. It was nothing special, really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it Stela who gave that you piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: I took a piece of paper from him too, because I asked him to write such a paper for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about having this shop and the need to operate this shop to repair vehicles. Were you acting during this time, sir, as a primarily as a soldier? Did you have a position on the Bulevar that you had to man? Or were you working in your shop during this time period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: I was considered to be a soldier, although I worked in the shop, but I did go to the line for maybe ten times, if there wasn't enough personnel. If they were short of men, then everybody from the logistics would go there because it happened quite often that they were short of men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you join the HVO, by the way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: From day one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if the HVO was first formed in approximately April, 1992, are you saying you joined the HVO in April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then how long did you continue to be a member of the HVO? When did you leave the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Until the last day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, sir, meaning what? The last day of what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: That means when the battalion was disbanded and no longer existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you can assist us a bit with the date. When did the unit disband? You don't have to give us the exact day but approximately when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I couldn't recall the exact date. It may have been -- but don't hold me to what I'm saying -- may have been 1994 or 1995. I don't remember, really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But it was well after 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But the documents exist and it shouldn't be a problem to determine the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was this document about your garage, the fact that it was used in a sense to assist the HVO, apart from that document, piece of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. paper that you said you obtained, to your knowledge, were any other papers -- for the purposes of protecting you, either given to you or your family or other Muslims in that area by Mr. Martinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: I had my military ID card. That was simply to protect this part of my property, because some people may have aspired to get the machinery, the tools that were there and on many occasions the house was empty. That was simply the reason why I needed that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving forward to the 9th of May, 1993 for a moment, were you with Mr. Martinovic that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: The 9th of May, yes, I met him in the early evening hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was that? Where were you located at the time you met him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: We met somewhere in Balinovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that just a coincidence that you met him or was there any other purpose to meeting Mr. Martinovic at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: It was just a coincidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct, sir, that that's the only time that you saw him on the day of May 9th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see him at all the next day, on the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: I don't think so. It's impossible for me now to remember everything. It was a really chaotic situation with the shooting everywhere. Everything was on fire. And it's really hard to notice things and to remember them later, little details, I mean. Half the people didn't know what was going on at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to be shown, please, exhibits -- if you can put them both before him at the same time because they are closely related 455.1 and 456.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We have not been provided --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LUI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we don't know what this is all about because we haven't been given anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, they are sitting here. My apologies. They should have been distributed, and by oversight, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, they should.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I refuse to accept them, I refuse to take them because we weren't given these documents on time, just before the cross-examination, and an order was issued to the Prosecution to that effect. And this was just before the break. I cannot now read this very fast, because I cannot then see whether I have any objections to them or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric, I believe that most of the documents have been used or admitted in this courtroom. And I understand that most of the witnesses are not political or high military officials, so I believe in this case, those documents will be used in a very limited way. Let us see how far the Prosecutor will go with those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would also say that 455.1 and 456.2 are both already admitted. They have been used with a number of witnesses. So I don't think there is any surprise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to look at both of those documents briefly, actually you can concentrate again to save time, you're welcome to look at both but if you could direct your attention to 456.2, and there is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President, but I really don't want to argue but as a matter of principle I want this to be entered into the record. I want to object to the fact that the Defence is not given documents on time. This is for the sake of the future of the proceedings and the future way that the Prosecution treats us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, in this aspect, I'm very sympathetic to you because we have a very long break after the first -- after the direct examination. So I believe that during that break, the Prosecution side had enough time to distribute those documents they intended to use during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to respond, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we had immediately gone to cross-examination, if we had immediately instead of going on a break, I had immediately stood up and asked my first question, the documents would have been distributed at that time. There would have been no additional time, no different than now. It would be no difference whatsoever between the time that counsel would have had the documents. I do apologise, as I've said, they were sitting right there, and it was an oversight that they weren't distributed during the break, and for that, counsel has my apology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you will look at, in the Croatian language version, I'd like you to look at the first paragraph and again 456.2. I'm going to read this to you and I'll ask you a few questions about it. "With reference to yesterday's incident, I can relate the following. After I sent the men to the line, I went to the command of the 1st Battalion. There I was received a report that men in uniforms were moving about --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down when reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "In zone 3, that is to say in the Dum complex of buildings, gathering Muslims in the buildings, firing and disturbing public law and order. I immediately went to the scene and encountered Stela with 40 soldiers. I asked one of them what they were doing. He said that they were there with Tuta -- excuse me, they were with Tuta, and that Tuta told them to gather all and send them to the other side." And this is a report concerning events on the 13th and 14th of June, 1993. Now, the area that's described as zone number 3, did that include any part of the Bulevar confrontation line, sir, where you said you were assigned as part of the 4th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The report, sir, makes reference to a zone 3, and if you know, did that include any part of the confrontation line for which your unit, the 4th Battalion, was responsible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Whether our unit was responsible for that area, if I understand your question correctly? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. For any part of zone 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not objecting to the document. I am objecting as to the foundation of the question, because this document is not the proper foundation for this question. It's obvious that the purpose why the Prosecution read out this document was completely different. He obviously needed this document for another purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult to judge the intention of the other party for us. Mr. Scott, you may proceed with your question, and then we'll arrive it at the conclusion, because it's very difficult for us to make any decisions on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President the issue of needing a document, the document is already --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to respond to counsel, the issue of me needing a document, the document is already in evidence, Mr. President. It's already in evidence. The Chamber, I believe, has seen both these documents before so it's not a question of needing the document. I wanted to ask the witness questions about it and that's what I've done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I go back to my question, sir, did the area of the 4th Battalion's responsibility on the confrontation line include anything that was described as zone 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me come at it this way. Are you familiar -- does the term "zone 3" mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Zone 3, would that be the health care centre? The medical centre?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I can't give that information to you. I can only ask you the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, you may ask this witness what his responsibility was -- what's the area of his responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President, we will approach it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What part of the confrontation line did you have any responsibility for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: The part of the confrontation line from Sipad to Aleksica, Aleksica's house. This is where it was more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps we should go to private session, in light of these difficulties, Mr. President. It might be helpful to have the aerial photograph again, the one that we were using before?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Actually I think not the aerial photograph but the street map, the 11.18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Are we ready? Witness MC, I believe you are, same as my initials so I should remember that, just on the last issue that you were describing, where you stood in for the person who normally brought the prisoners from the Heliodrom, who was away for a few days, you described to Mr. Scott how you just collected the prisoners and then later on you returned them. Do you recall did you bring them to the same place every day for the few days that you stood in for your colleague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Same place, same place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And was that the front line at your battalion -- sorry, the front line of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: From the Heliodrom, I took them to the battalion, to the battalion. And after that, I had nothing to do with them. I do my job in my workshop. 15, 20 minutes, half an hour, 7, 8 o'clock, depends, I mean when they call me, get leer to take them back, and that was my job for those three, four, five days. But the name or man, names, I can't remember the name of any man. And there is no way I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Witness MC, that's quite understandable. I don't think that's what Mr. Scott was asking you, whether you knew the names. But what I'm asking you now, and I think he was trying to ask you, when you went to collect the detainees that you'd left at the 4th Battalion, was there any system in operation whereby you would count them back or you'd have any document to fill in that the same number that you brought returned in the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Now, how shall I explain it to you? When the deputy commander, commander, captain, whoever was responsible for them there, he was the one who kept the count. My job was along side, that is my job, you also drive them, drive them up, drive them down. Anything else, I really cannot speak about anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm wandering back over your evidence. You explained to us, Witness MC, that you were in the HVO long before the conflict began on the 9th of May. Can you tell me, because of your experience -- I know you were in logistics -- but was the confrontation line not already in existence before the 9th of May? This one on the Bulevar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So when did it -- when was it determined? Its location, when was that determined?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: After the 9th. After the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Very good. Now, --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: At least from what I know. Because you see, I was a soldier first of all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I accept that your understanding is that the confrontation line only came into existence after the 9th of May. Now, if I move to a different issue, Witness MC, we are becoming familiar with the various names and first names of the various ethnic Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. groups in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I think that I would recognise very easily that yours is a Muslim name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: We've heard evidence from a number of people, that doesn't mean it's correct, but we've heard this evidence, that Muslim members of the HVO, who were many originally, were in fact disarmed and arrested, as the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims progressed. How did you escape that particular fate? If you think my question is too personal, you can say so, but if it's a question you're prepared to help us with --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Quite all right. In that unit, Muslims who wanted to do so, moved -- crossed over to the BH Army. Those who didn't want to, stayed on and nobody harmed them. I was born there. My home was there. So it was natural for me to stay on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And as you were describing earlier, you felt quite safe, as a Muslim, in this particular battalion. Now, my question is: Would that generally have been known in the area where you lived, that you, as a Muslim, were a card-carrying member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: But of course it was known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And the reason I ask you that was that I was wondering did any of your Muslim neighbours or friends, who were not in the HVO come to you for protection because of your position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: To begin with, I had no position to speak of. I was just a foot soldier who worked in a workshop, and all the other Muslims from my street, without any IDs or anything, they stayed there throughout the war and are still there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So it's your position that even though you were a foot soldier in the HVO, you were in no position to afford any protection to your Muslim neighbours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MC
utterances.text: Well, I had no need to. I don't know what kind of protection. Everything was more or less normal. Not only Muslims. Croats, Muslims and Serbs, those who were left, nobody was indifferent. Ever was afraid of all these groups and gangs. You have, countless examples when the Croats were robbed and as I said in the beginning, my friend, he's a Croat, his mother was robbed. Nobody could say, "I am safe." But then somehow one managed, one squeezed through, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That's all my questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judges question? Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do not. I would have nodded but I cannot because of all these binders but I do not have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, thank you very much for coming leer to help us. We appreciate it very much. The usher will show you out of the room. We all wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: During the direct examination, the document P14.5, which was a photo of the front line, was used and marked by the witness. Now it became the D2/29, if I'm not mistaken. It's admitted into evidence because it's a photo. In cross-examination, P11.18, a street map of Mostar was used and marked by the witness. Because this map is used in this courtroom, it is admitted into the evidence. Under seal. Are there any other documents would you like to tender, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I think on this occasion I think perhaps we can do this more quickly. The number for the marked copy of P11.18, Madam Registrar? 15/15? Yes, Your Honour, in addition to that one, the only -- I think the only other two that were used that were previously not admitted were 609.3 and 612.3, both of which come from the Zagreb archive and have quite clearly possess the stamp from the archive and we would tender those two additional documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, will you give us sometime to respond to the -- these two documents which were tender by the Prosecution? Of course, I mean these two new documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, but you have to did it as soon as possible because there are only two documents. Thank you. Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The accused Naletilic would object to 609.3 and also to P612.3 on the grounds that this witness specifically and clearly testified he had no clue about the detainees who were allegedly wounded when they were returned. He explained what his job was during the few days that the normal driver was elsewhere. His job was not to look after the prisoners nor was his job to count the prisoners or count heads. Judge Clark's question made that quite clear. This witness could shed no light on these two documents other than he admitted, yes, he took the prisoners and he brought them back. Now the relevance of these documents for the Prosecution, I believe, is the fact that the documents indicate in writing that one or two of the prisoners, upon return to the Heliodrom, were injured. The witness quite specifically and clearly stated he didn't know anything about that handwriting. The handwriting -- there is no evidence the handwriting was put on in his presence. He never observed any wounded prisoners, so there is no foundation. It's irrelevant and there is no probative value and we object, object all of those grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take your objections into consideration when we consider the admission of those documents after we received the written submissions from the Defence counsel for Martinovic at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And for the record, Mr. President, we would join in with any further objections by the counsel for Mr. Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the sake of time could I just -- can I please respond now because counsel has not correctly stated our position. The main reason, in fact, that they were tendered was because initially the witness denied having any involvement with prisoners whatsoever. And in fact, while he didn't -- I believe it's a fair statement that while he didn't recall the facts about any particular witness being wounded or captured, he did not in fact deny that he was involved in fact when confronted with the documents that he was in fact involved with transporting them back and forth. Therefore, it is directly relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, your view is registered in the transcript. We also would like to take into consideration at a later stage. But now we are not debating this issue. Your views are all there, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, my view is not there because if that is the point of the admission of these two document by my learned friend, then the record is very clear that the question asked of this witness, "Was he involved in taking detainees for forced labour"? This witness specifically testified that the people that were taken out were not used for forced labour. In fact they requested to be taken out. And there is a very big difference. The record is clear, the question was for forced labour. It was obvious the witness answered no, not to forced labour. Voluntary labour is a different thing than forced labour. So that's our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid we have to spend a whole afternoon debating on the testimony of this witness so we will leave it to a later stage. Yes, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I would just like to inform both parties that it's very important that you let me know if a document is confidential or under seal when it's pertaining to a witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's time for a break. We hope that we could hear the next witness after the break. We will resume at 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could we have the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Par:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, ma'am. Before we begin with our conversation, I would like to tell you that the Trial Chamber has granted the protective measures for you so that your identity will be completely protected and parts of the testimony which might lead to revealing of your identity will be conducted in closed session. Let me just warn you right at the beginning that you have to speak slowly because of the interpretation, and not to answer my question immediately, but only when the red light on my microphone has been switched off. This is the time when you should start answering my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to request that we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will begin this examination with the beginning of the Serb aggression on Mostar. How old were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who did you live with at the time but don't mention any names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MD
utterances.text: With my parents and my sisters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, at the time of the Serb aggression on the town, did anything happen to you in particular or did you just have to live through that period? We don't have to dwell too long on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MD
utterances.text: No, nothing in particular happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, at that time, so that's the very beginning with the war with the Serbs, did you know Vinko Martinovic, Stela? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MD
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly how did you know him? How well did you know him? What kind of terms were you on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MD
utterances.text: Since we lived in the same neighbourhood, we knew each other from before, although we are not of the same generation. When the war began, I went -- I was going to school and we would see each other. He would drive me to school. Sometimes, and that's how we became friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell us, at this time, when the war with the Serbs was going on, was he involved militarily in it? Was he a member of any military unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MD
utterances.text: Yes. He was a member of HOS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if he held any posts in HOS or anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MD
utterances.text: Well he was one of the commanders in HOS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what was his attitude towards Muslim Bosniaks at the time? How did he treat them? Is there anything particular about the way he treated them? Was there any difference between the way he treated Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MD
utterances.text: No, no. There was no difference. He acted normally. He treated people as friends and acquaintances if they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we will move on to this other conflict that happened in Mostar after the conflict with the Serbs and that's the conflict between Croats and Muslims. Do you remember that day and if you do, could you please tell us when it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MD
utterances.text: It was on the 9th of May, 1993. That's when it began.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly how did you and your family experience that day? What happened to you? Give us a picture of the events for you and your family.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MD
utterances.text: Well, we were at home. It happened at around 5.20 in the morning, shooting began. Nobody knew anything. Nobody even guessed what was happening. We were at home and then soldiers came. They asked for our documents. And then they took us out, all of us. My younger sister was crying. She was seven at the time. She was crying and she was begging one of the soldiers, "Please, sir, don't kill us." And then he took my mother and my sister back into the apartment and then myself, my older sister and my father followed them. The rest remained lined up in front of the building. One of the neighbours from Gornja street, a Croat, came out and started swearing and cursing us, cursing, saying, "What are you doing? I have to continue to living with these people? Not you. You can't do it like this." And everybody was taken back to their apartments. Nobody was expelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that they were soldiers. Do you know which soldiers these were? Did you recognise anyone? Do you know what formation they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MD
utterances.text: No. I didn't recognise anyone. They were just soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are being warned that we will have to speak a bit slower. So I understand you correctly, you didn't know those soldiers and you didn't know what unit they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that in the end, all the citizens who had been taken out of the building were brought back. My question is who lived in the building? Were they Croats, Muslims? What was the proportion, the ratio of ethnicities in your building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MD
utterances.text: There were Croats, Muslims, three Croat apartments and four Muslim apartments. One apartment was empty. Nobody lived there. We were all taken out. Regardless of our ethnic background. And fortunately we were all then allowed to go back or brought back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that your family remained there throughout the war. Did the other Muslim families also remain there throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During those days, did you see Vinko Martinovic, Stela? I mean around the time when the conflict broke out, the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MD
utterances.text: Not before but afterwards, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how did you see him? What happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MD
utterances.text: I had my grandmother, who lived in Djikovina. That was one street below from us. I didn't know what was with her. Vinko came to see what was happening with us, how we were. I asked him if we could go to the apartment, to check whether my grandmother was there. But she wasn't because she had been expelled to the east side of the town. I spoke to Vinko then. He said that I shouldn't be afraid, that nothing would happen to anyone from our street, that he would try to come or send one of his boys, because we all knew each other, to prevent any other people from coming and coming and from persecuting us and, and that's how it happened. Nobody showed up in our street any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me, you said that either he would come or some of his soldiers would come. Did you know his soldiers to know that they belonged to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MD
utterances.text: Yes, I did know them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
